params.title: RADAR Principles
params.subtitle: How a ship's radar finds a target, the timing and power math behind it, its main parts, and the circuits in Figures 8A1 to 8A8.

onScreen: Radar parts and the circuits in Figures 8A1 to 8A8
scenes.narration: Welcome to RADAR principles, the first lesson of Element 8. A ship's radar sees other ships, buoys and coastlines in fog and darkness, and as a radar technician you'll be the one who keeps it working. You don't need any background in electricity or radar. We'll start from scratch with how radar finds a target: a short burst of radio energy goes out, an echo comes back, and the timing tells the distance. Then we'll add the pulse timing, power and wavelength calculations, the main parts of a radar set, and the circuits in the exam's Figures 8A1 through 8A8. By the end, you'll be able to work every calculation and explain why each answer is right.

blocks.label: Radar sends a pulse
blocks.note: A short burst of radio energy

blocks.label: Echo returns
blocks.note: A tiny part of the energy

onScreen: Radar sends a short pulse of radio energy
The wait time gives the range
scenes.narration: Start with an echo. Shout toward a cliff, and a moment later you hear your voice come back. The farther away the cliff, the longer you wait. Radar works the same way, using radio waves instead of sound. The name RADAR stands for radio detection and ranging, and ranging means measuring distance. The radar sends out a short burst of radio energy called a pulse. When the pulse hits a ship, a buoy or a coastline, a tiny part of its energy bounces back toward the radar. That returning signal is the echo. The radar measures how long the echo took to come back, and from that wait time it works out the range, the distance to the target.

params.title: How fast a radio wave travels
items: A radio wave: electric and magnetic energy traveling through space
It moves at the speed of light
Microsecond (µs): one millionth of a second
Radio waves cover about 300 meters every microsecond

onScreen: Radio wave: electric and magnetic energy
Travels at the speed of light
Microsecond: one millionth of a second
scenes.narration: So what is a radio wave? It's energy traveling through space as a ripple of electric and magnetic force. It belongs to the same family as light, just invisible to us, and it travels at the same speed: the speed of light. That's so fast that radar timing is measured in microseconds. A microsecond is one millionth of a second. In 1 microsecond, a radio wave travels about 300 meters. Hold on to that number, because it's the key to every range calculation in this lesson.

params.title: Meters of range per microsecond
steps: A radio wave travels about 300 meters per µs
The echo goes out and back: divide by 2

scenes.narration: Now the catch. The echo has to make 2 trips: out to the target and back again. In 1 microsecond the wave covers 300 meters, but that's 150 meters out and 150 meters back. So each microsecond of waiting means the target is 150 meters farther away: 300 meters divided by 2. That's the constant the exam asks for: RADAR range is measured by the constant 150 meters per microsecond. Watch the units. The trap answers offer 150 yards and 300 yards per microsecond. The correct one is meters, and it's 150, not 300, because of that round trip.

params.title: Range and bearing on the screen
labels: The echo: its distance from the center gives the range
Bearing: the direction the antenna faced when the echo came back
Range rings: circles at equal steps of distance

onScreen: Echo: distance from the center is the range
Bearing: the direction the antenna faced
scenes.narration: Distance is only half the picture. The radar also needs direction. Its antenna keeps turning, sending pulses in a narrow beam, like a lighthouse sweeping its light across the sea. The screen, called the indicator, puts your ship at the center, and a line turns in step with the antenna. When an echo comes back, it's painted as a spot along that line. How far the spot sits from the center shows the range. The direction of the line shows the bearing: the direction the antenna was facing, measured in degrees clockwise from north or from the ship's heading, like a compass. Circles called range rings mark equal steps of distance, so you can read the range at a glance.

params.title: The RADAR mile
labels: A target 1 nautical mile away
Out and back: 12.34 µs
That round trip time is 1 RADAR mile

scenes.narration: Those range rings are marked in nautical miles, the unit of distance at sea, a little longer than the land mile. To go with it, radar technicians use a handy unit of time called the RADAR mile. Picture a target exactly 1 nautical mile away. The pulse races out to it, the echo races back, and the whole round trip takes 12.34 microseconds. That time is 1 RADAR mile. It comes straight from our 150 meters per microsecond: a nautical mile divided by 150 meters per microsecond works out to about 12.34 microseconds. Memorize 12.34. It's the most used number in this lesson, and the exam asks for it directly. The trap answer 6.2 is only the one-way time.

params.title: One way: half a RADAR mile
params.formula: One way per nm = 12.34 µs ÷ 2 ≈ 6.17 µs

onScreen: One way: about 6.17 µs per nautical mile
scenes.narration: Sometimes the exam asks about a one-way trip, with no echo coming back. The RADAR mile covers out and back, so one way takes half as long: 12.34 divided by 2, about 6.17 microseconds per nautical mile. Here's the question: how long does a radio wave take to travel 3 nautical miles? It's one way, so use 6.17. 3 times 6.17 microseconds is 18.51 microseconds. There are 2 traps: 6.17 microseconds is the time for just 1 mile, and 37.0 microseconds is what you'd get by using the round trip 12.34 by mistake.

Now the round trip, which is what a radar actually measures. Each nautical mile of range adds 1 RADAR mile of waiting. So the echo time, t, equals the range in nautical miles times 12.34 microseconds. A target 5 miles away: 5 times 12.34 microseconds is 61.7 microseconds. A target 10 nautical miles away: 10 times 12.34 is 123.4 microseconds. Does that make sense? Twice as far, twice the wait. On the 10 mile question, watch for 12.34 and 1.234 microseconds as traps: the first is the time for just 1 mile, and the second has a misplaced decimal point.

params.title: Range from echo time
steps: Echo time t = 308.5 µs, out and back
No halving: 12.34 µs is already a round trip

scenes.narration: The radar does the opposite: it measures the echo time and works out the range. Just turn the formula around. Range, R, equals the echo time divided by 12.34 microseconds. Suppose a pulse takes 308.5 microseconds to travel to a target and back. 308.5 divided by 12.34 is 25, so the target is 25 nautical miles away. Here's the trap. The question says the time covers the trip to the target and back, and it's tempting to halve it first. Don't: the 12.34 microsecond RADAR mile already includes the return trip. Halving would give 12.5 miles, only half the true range.

params.title: Pulses: talk, then listen
labels: Pulse: the transmitter switched on for a brief moment
Pulse width: how long each pulse lasts
Between pulses: the radar listens for echoes

onScreen: Pulse width: how long each pulse lasts
scenes.narration: So far we've timed a single pulse and its echo. But a radar never sends just one. Back to the cliff: if you shouted nonstop, you'd never hear the echo. So you shout once, then listen. Radar does the same, hundreds or thousands of times a second. Here's what that looks like over time. The transmitter switches on for a brief moment, sending a pulse, then switches off and waits. The length of each pulse is called the pulse width, and it's tiny: in the exam's examples, from 0.05 to 1 microsecond. Between pulses, the transmitter is silent, and the radar listens for echoes. This picture is called a pulse train, and we'll come back to it often.

params.title: How often the pulses repeat
labels: PRF, or PRR: pulses sent per second, in hertz
Pulse period, or PRI: start of one pulse to start of the next
PRI = 1 ÷ PRF

onScreen: PRF or PRR: pulses per second
scenes.narration: How often does the radar send a pulse? That rate is the pulse repetition frequency, or PRF. It's also called the pulse repetition rate, or PRR: 2 names for the same thing. It's measured in hertz, and 1 hertz means once per second, so a PRF of 1000 hertz means 1000 pulses every second. The time from the start of one pulse to the start of the next is the pulse period, which the exam also calls the pulse repetition interval, or PRI. PRF and PRI are flip sides: the more pulses per second, the less time each one gets. At 1000 pulses a second, each gets a thousandth of a second. In symbols, PRI equals 1 divided by PRF.

Let's work 2 exam questions. If the PRF is 2500 hertz, what is the PRI? Think of 1 second shared equally among 2,500 pulses. Each pulse gets 1 divided by 2,500 of a second, which is 0.0004 seconds. To turn seconds into microseconds, multiply by a million: 0.0004 seconds is 400 microseconds. Second question: a PRF of 2000 hertz. 1 divided by 2,000 is 0.0005 seconds, or 500 microseconds. That question wants seconds, so pick 0.0005 seconds, and watch for the traps with an extra or missing zero, such as 0.005 or 0.00005 seconds.

params.title: Duty cycle
labels: Duty cycle: the fraction of time the transmitter is on
Duty cycle = pulse width ÷ pulse period
The same thing: duty cycle = PW × PRF

onScreen: Duty cycle: fraction of time on
scenes.narration: So the PRF says how often the transmitter fires. But how much of the time is it actually on? That fraction is called the duty cycle. Picture someone who says a single word, then listens for a whole minute: they're talking only a tiny fraction of the time. To find the duty cycle, divide the pulse width by the pulse period. Since the PRF is 1 divided by the pulse period, dividing by the pulse period is the same as multiplying by the PRF. So duty cycle also equals the pulse width, PW, times the PRF, and that's the form the exam uses. Duty cycle has no units: it's just a fraction, usually a very small one.

params.title: Duty cycle, worked
steps: On time per second: 2,000 × 0.05 µs = 100 µs

scenes.narration: Let's try one. A radar has a PRF of 2000 hertz and a pulse width of 0.05 microseconds. What's the duty cycle? First, a word about 10 to the minus 6. It's the exam's way of writing one millionth, so 0.05 microseconds is 0.05 times 10 to the minus 6 seconds. Duty cycle is PW times PRF, and here's what that multiplication means. Think about 1 second of operation. The radar fires 2,000 pulses, each 0.05 microseconds long, so it's on for 2,000 times 0.05, or 100 microseconds in total. 100 microseconds out of the million microseconds in a second is 0.0001. So the duty cycle is 0.0001: the transmitter is on only one ten-thousandth of the time.

The exam's version adds some distractions. A transmitter has a PRF of 1,000 hertz, a pulse width of 0.5 microseconds, a peak power of 150 kilowatts and a minimum range of 75 meters. What's its duty cycle? Peak power, the strength of each pulse, and minimum range, how close the radar can see, come later, and you don't need them here. Duty cycle needs only pulse width and PRF. 0.5 times 10 to the minus 6 seconds, times 1,000 hertz, is 0.0005. As a check, each second, 1,000 pulses of 0.5 microseconds add up to 500 microseconds of on time, and 500 out of a million is 0.0005. The traps, 0.5, 0.05 and 0.005, all misplace the decimal point.

params.title: The 4 main parts of a radar

scenes.narration: You now know what radar measures and how its pulses are timed. Let's look at the equipment that does it. A radar set has 4 main parts. The transmitter makes the powerful radio pulses. The antenna, on its turning mount high on the mast, sends each pulse out in a narrow beam and catches the echoes that come back. The receiver takes those echoes, which are extremely weak, and amplifies them, meaning it makes them much stronger. And the indicator, the screen, shows the targets. Over the next few scenes we'll look inside each part, starting with what drives them all: electricity.

params.title: Voltage, current and power
items: Current: the flow of electric charge, measured in amperes (amps)
Voltage: the push that drives the current, measured in volts
Power: how fast energy is delivered, measured in watts
Watts = volts × amps; 1 kilowatt (kW) = 1000 watts

onScreen: Power: energy per second, in watts
scenes.narration: Every radar part runs on electricity, so here are 3 basic ideas. Picture water flowing through a pipe. Current is the flow itself: how much electric charge moves past a point each second. That charge is carried by electrons, tiny particles found in every atom. Current is measured in amperes, or amps. Voltage is the push, like water pressure, that drives the current along, and it's measured in volts. Power is how fast energy is delivered, like how hard the water works as it turns a mill wheel. It's measured in watts: volts times amps. A kilowatt, kilo meaning a thousand, is 1000 watts. To make strong pulses, a radar transmitter works with thousands of volts.

blocks.label: Synchronizer
blocks.note: Also called timer or trigger generator

blocks.label: Magnetron
blocks.note: Turns it into a radio pulse

blocks.label: Indicator
blocks.note: Starts its sweep at the same instant

onScreen: Same trigger starts the indicator sweep
scenes.narration: First, the radar's clock. The synchronizer, also called the timer or trigger generator, controls timing throughout the RADAR system. Each time a pulse is due, it sends out a short timing pulse called a trigger. The trigger fires the modulator, a switch that dumps a big burst of high voltage into the magnetron for exactly 1 pulse width. The magnetron is the tube that turns that burst into a pulse of radio energy. At the same instant, the same trigger starts the indicator's sweep, the spot moving out from the screen's center, and the range circuits, so range timing starts as the pulse leaves. On the exam, the synchronizer, not the power supply or the indicator, controls the timing.

callouts.label: Cathode: when hot, it gives off electrons
Filament: the heater that keeps the cathode hot
Anode: a copper block around the cathode
Magnet: bends the electrons into a spinning cloud
Cavities: ring at a microwave frequency, like whistles
Output: a pulse each time it fires; the PRR is its firing rate

scenes.narration: Let's look inside the magnetron. It's a vacuum tube: a sealed metal case with the air pumped out. At its center is the cathode, which gives off electrons when it's hot. A small heater called the filament keeps it hot. Around it is a solid copper block, the anode, cut with a ring of small cavities. A strong magnet bends the electrons into a spinning cloud as they're pulled toward the anode. As they sweep past, the cavities ring like whistles at a microwave frequency, vibrating billions of times a second. The magnetron fires once for each pulse from the modulator. So the pulse repetition rate is the pulse rate of the magnetron: how many times per second it's fired.

callouts.label: Anode: grounded
Cathode: pulsed to a high negative voltage
Filament: tied to the cathode, so it rides at that voltage
The filament carries dangerous voltages

scenes.narration: One safety point while we're looking at the magnetron. Which part of it carries dangerous voltage? You might guess the anode, but in a radar magnetron the anode is grounded, connected to the metal frame. The modulator's high voltage pulse goes to the cathode instead, driving it to a high negative voltage. Now remember the filament, the little heater for the cathode. It's built right onto the cathode and connected to it, so the whole filament circuit rides at that same high voltage. So the filament of the magnetron carries dangerous voltages. On the exam, don't fall for the idea that the filament is a low voltage circuit just because it's a heater.

onScreen: Duplexer: one antenna for transmit and receive
During the pulse: energy to the antenna
Between pulses: echoes to the receiver
scenes.narration: The pulse leaves the magnetron, heading for the antenna. But that same antenna must also catch the echoes. The duplexer is what allows a single antenna to be used for both transmitting and receiving. During each pulse, it routes the magnetron's energy to the antenna and blocks the path to the receiver, which the full pulse would burn out. Between pulses, it switches back and passes the weak echoes down to the receiver, like a railway switch flipping thousands of times a second. The wrong choices each have another job: the synchronizer sets the timing, the modulator powers the magnetron, and the mixer is part of the receiver, as you'll see next.

params.title: The receiver and its local oscillator

blocks.label: Mixer
blocks.note: Shifts the echo to a lower frequency

onScreen: Mixer shifts them lower in frequency
Local oscillator runs continuously, not pulsed
scenes.narration: That's the transmitter side. Now follow the echo in. From the duplexer, the weak echo goes to the receiver's mixer. There it's combined with a steady signal from a small oscillator inside the receiver, called the local oscillator. An oscillator is a circuit that makes a continuous radio wave on its own. Mixing shifts the echo down to a lower frequency, a slower vibration, which amplifiers can build up far more easily. Here's an exam point: the local oscillator, whether a klystron tube or a solid-state device, meaning a small chip rather than a tube, runs continuously. It is never pulsed. So the pulse repetition rate refers to the magnetron, not to the local oscillator or the klystron.

params.title: A sweep for every pulse
labels: Each pulse starts one sweep from the center outward
Echoes are painted along the sweep as they arrive
Sweeps per second = pulses per second
Indicator sweep frequency is set by the PRF

onScreen: Sweeps per second = pulses per second
Sweep frequency set by the PRF
scenes.narration: Last stop: the indicator. The synchronizer starts it at the same instant each pulse leaves, and a spot moves steadily out from the center of the screen along the line: that's 1 sweep. The sawtooth shows the spot climbing, then snapping back for the next pulse. Echoes are painted along the sweep as they arrive, so a later echo lands farther out. Since each pulse triggers 1 sweep, there are as many sweeps per second as pulses per second. So the sweep frequency of a RADAR indicator is set by the pulse repetition frequency. The carrier frequency, the frequency of the radio wave itself, doesn't decide how often the trace restarts, and nor do pulse width or duty cycle.

params.title: Frequency: cycles per second
labels: 1 cycle: a complete swing of the wave
Frequency: cycles per second, in hertz
Kilohertz: thousands. Megahertz: millions. Gigahertz: billions
Carrier frequency: the radio wave inside each pulse

onScreen: Carrier frequency: the wave inside each pulse
scenes.narration: That completes the tour of the radar's parts. We've said the magnetron makes microwaves. What does that really mean? A radio wave vibrates, swinging back and forth like this. A complete swing is called a cycle, and the number of cycles each second is the wave's frequency, measured in hertz. A kilohertz is a thousand hertz, a megahertz is a million, and a gigahertz is a billion. A radar's radio wave vibrates billions of times a second. That's called the carrier frequency, because the wave carries the pulse. Don't mix it up with the PRF. A single pulse holds hundreds or thousands of carrier cycles, while the pulses themselves come far less often: hundreds or thousands per second.

params.title: Where radar sits in the radio spectrum

scenes.narration: Radio waves come in a huge range of frequencies, called the radio spectrum, and it's divided into bands, each 10 times higher in frequency than the last. VHF, very high frequency, runs from 30 to 300 megahertz: that's where ship-to-ship voice radio lives. UHF, ultra high frequency, runs from 300 megahertz to 3 gigahertz. Next comes SHF, super high frequency, from 3 to 30 gigahertz. Frequencies generally used for marine RADAR are in the SHF part of the spectrum, mainly near 3 gigahertz and near 9.4 gigahertz. Above that is EHF, extremely high frequency. On the exam, VHF, UHF and EHF are the wrong choices: marine radar is SHF.

params.title: Wavelength
labels: Wavelength (λ): the distance the wave travels in one cycle
λ = c ÷ f: speed of light divided by frequency
Higher frequency: shorter wavelength

scenes.narration: Besides its frequency, every radio wave also has a length. While the wave completes 1 cycle, it moves forward a certain distance. That distance is the wavelength, written with the Greek letter lambda. Think of ocean waves: the wavelength is the distance from one crest to the next. To find it, divide the speed of the wave by its frequency. For radio waves, the speed is the speed of light, written c. So lambda equals c divided by f, where f is the frequency. The more cycles squeezed into each second, the shorter each one must be. So the higher the frequency, the shorter the wavelength.

Let's find the wavelength of a RADAR operating at 3 gigahertz. The speed of light, c, is 3 times 10 to the power 8 meters per second: a 3 followed by 8 zeros, or 300 million meters every second, the same as our 300 meters per microsecond. The frequency, 3 gigahertz, is 3 times 10 to the power 9 hertz, a 3 followed by 9 zeros. Divide: the 3s cancel, and 10 to the 8 over 10 to the 9 leaves one tenth. So lambda is 0.1 meter, or 10 centimeters. Radar near 3 gigahertz is called S-band, as you'll see next, which is why S-band is often called 10-centimeter radar. The traps are 1, 3 and 30 centimeters.

marks.label: S-band: 2 to 4 GHz
marks.note: 15 to 7.5 cm; marine sets near 3 GHz

marks.label: X-band: 8 to 12 GHz
marks.note: Marine sets near 9.4 GHz: about 3.2 cm

scenes.narration: Radar engineers name their bands with letters. An S-band RADAR operates in the 2 to 4 gigahertz band, with wavelengths from about 15 down to 7.5 centimeters, and marine S-band sets typically run near 3 gigahertz, our 10-centimeter radar. An X-band RADAR operates in the 8 to 12 gigahertz band. Marine X-band sets usually transmit near 9.4 gigahertz, a wavelength of about 3.2 centimeters. Notice the pattern: X-band's frequency is about 3 times higher, so its wavelength is about 3 times shorter. The exam offers 1 to 2 and 4 to 8 gigahertz as traps in both questions. Remember: S is 2 to 4, X is 8 to 12.

params.title: Why radar uses microwaves
items: Microwaves: wavelengths of a few centimeters
They're used so that stronger target echoes are produced
Reason 1: ships, buoys and coastlines are huge compared with the wave
Reason 2: a practical-size antenna can form a narrow, high-gain beam

onScreen: Targets much bigger than the wave reflect strongly
scenes.narration: Why such high frequencies? Waves just a few centimeters long are called microwaves. Practical RADAR operation requires microwave frequencies so that stronger target echoes will be produced, for 2 reasons. First, a wave bounces best off objects much bigger than its wavelength: long ocean swells roll right past a thin post, but small ripples bounce off it. A ship, a buoy or a coastline is huge compared with a 3 centimeter wave, so it reflects strongly. Second, an antenna of practical size can form a narrow, high-gain beam, concentrating the energy like a flashlight's reflector. Less ground clutter, the unwanted echoes from land, and less interference aren't the reason, and radar needs a sharply directional antenna, not a non-directional one.

So which band is better? Each has a strength. S-band runs from 2 to 4 gigahertz, about 10 centimeters, and X-band from 8 to 12 gigahertz, about 3 centimeters. The major advantage of an S-band RADAR over an X-band RADAR is that it is less affected by weather conditions. Rain, snow and fog scatter and absorb short waves far more than long ones, so S-band's longer waves get through bad weather much better. X-band wins on bearing resolution: showing 2 targets side by side at the same range as 2 separate echoes. Its shorter waves give a narrower beam from the same size antenna. So the S-band advantage is weather, not bearing resolution, mechanical simplicity or greater power.

params.title: Peak power and average power
labels: Peak power: the power during the pulse itself
Between pulses: no power at all
Average power: the pulse power spread over the whole period
Average power is measured over a period of time

onScreen: Average power: spread over the period
scenes.narration: So much for the radio wave inside each pulse. Now, how strong is each pulse? There are 2 ways to state a radar's power. Peak power is the power during the brief pulse itself, and it's large: often many kilowatts. But between pulses, the transmitter sends nothing at all. If you spread each pulse's energy evenly over the whole pulse period, you get the average power, which is far lower. It's like a camera flash: blindingly bright for an instant, but over a whole minute it gives very little light. So when the exam asks what type of transmitter power is measured over a period of time, the answer is average power, not peak.

onScreen: P avg = P pk × PW × PRF
scenes.narration: How do you calculate average power? Multiply the peak power by the duty cycle. Since duty cycle is PW times PRF, P sub average equals P sub peak times PW times PRF. Here's the exam's question: a PRF of 400 hertz, a pulse width of 1 microsecond, and a peak power of 100 kilowatts. Step 1: convert to plain units. 100 kilowatts is 100,000 watts, and 1 microsecond is 1 times 10 to the minus 6 seconds. Step 2: the duty cycle, 1 times 10 to the minus 6, times 400, is 0.0004. Step 3: 100,000 watts times 0.0004 is 40 watts. That makes sense: on only 0.0004 of the time, a 100 kilowatt pulse averages just 40 watts.

Same steps, new numbers. A RADAR transmitter has a PRF of 900 hertz, a pulse width of 0.5 microseconds, and a peak power of 15 kilowatts. What's its average power output? First, 15 kilowatts is 15,000 watts. Next, the duty cycle: 0.5 times 10 to the minus 6 seconds, times 900 hertz, is 0.00045. Finally, 15,000 watts times 0.00045 is 6.75 watts. Does it make sense? The transmitter is on less than a thousandth of the time, so the average should be far below the peak, and it is. Watch for 2 traps: 13.5 watts is what you'd get using a 1 microsecond pulse, and 15 kilowatts is the peak, not the average.

params.title: Average power and duty cycle together

scenes.narration: One more. A RADAR set has a PRF of 1000 hertz, a pulse width of 1 microsecond, and a peak power rating of 100 kilowatts. What's the average power? The duty cycle is 1 times 10 to the minus 6 seconds, times 1,000 hertz, which is 0.001: on one thousandth of the time. 100,000 watts times 0.001 is 100 watts. Notice the shortcut: 1000 pulses of 1 microsecond add up to 1000 microseconds, a thousandth of a second, so the average is a thousandth of the peak. The traps, 10 and 1,000 watts, are each off by a factor of 10.

params.title: Average power from the pulse period

onScreen: P avg = P pk × PW ÷ pulse period
scenes.narration: Sometimes the exam gives you the pulse period instead of the PRF. A pulse RADAR transmits a 0.5 microsecond pulse with a peak power of 100 kilowatts every 1600 microseconds. Which statement about it is true? Since duty cycle is pulse width divided by pulse period, average power is peak power times pulse width, divided by the pulse period. The peak power is 100,000 watts and the pulse width 0.5 microseconds. The pulse period is 1,600 microseconds. So 100,000 watts times 0.5 microseconds, divided by 1,600 microseconds, gives 31.25 watts. The microseconds cancel out, leaving watts. That's the keyed answer: an average power of 31.25 watts.

params.title: Checking the other choices
items: Duty cycle = 0.5 ÷ 1,600 = 0.03125 percent, not 3.125 percent
480 km is a one-way trip in 1,600 µs: the echo must come back
Only the average power, 31.25 W, is right

scenes.narration: The other 3 choices are traps, and each is worth checking. A PRF of 3,200? The PRF is 1 divided by the pulse period. A second is a million microseconds, and a million divided by 1,600 is 625 hertz, not 3,200. A duty cycle of 3.125 percent? The duty cycle is 0.5 divided by 1,600, only 0.03125 percent. And a maximum range of 480 kilometers? That's how far a wave travels one way in 1,600 microseconds, at 300 meters per microsecond. It forgets that the echo must come back. So only the average power, 31.25 watts, is right.

params.title: Working backward to peak power
steps: P<sub>avg</sub> = 18 W, PW = 1 µs, PRF = 900 Hz

scenes.narration: The formula also works backward. If average power is peak power times duty cycle, then peak power is average power divided by duty cycle. A search RADAR has a pulse width of 1.0 microsecond, a PRF of 900 hertz, and an average power of 18 watts. What's its peak power? First the duty cycle: 1 times 10 to the minus 6 seconds, times 900 hertz, is 0.0009. Then divide: 18 watts divided by 0.0009 is 20,000 watts, or 20 kilowatts. Check it by working forward: 20,000 watts times 0.0009 gives back exactly 18 watts. The other choices, 2, 180 and 200 kilowatts, fail that check.

params.title: Wait for the echo before the next pulse
labels: Each echo must return before the next pulse fires
Pulse period ≥ round trip time to the farthest target
Round trip t = range × 12.34 µs, so PRF ≤ 1 ÷ t

onScreen: Echo returns before the next pulse
Pulse period at least the round trip time
scenes.narration: That's what the pulses cost in power. Let's see how their timing limits range. Picture the radar set to look 5 miles out. After each pulse, it must wait for echoes from as far as 5 miles before firing again. If the next pulse fires too soon, a distant echo arrives after the new sweep has started, and the screen paints it close in, at the wrong range. So each echo must return before the next pulse fires: the pulse period must be at least the round trip time to the farthest range, t equals range times 12.34 microseconds. And since PRF is 1 divided by the pulse period, the PRF must be no more than 1 divided by t.

For a range of 5 nautical miles, what should the PRF be? Step 1: the round trip time. 5 times 12.34 microseconds is 61.7 microseconds. Step 2: how many of those 61.7 microsecond waits fit into 1 second? A second is a million microseconds, and a million divided by 61.7 is about 16.2 thousand. So the radar can fire at most about 16.2 thousand pulses per second: 16.2 kilohertz. Step 3: the direction. It's a maximum, so the answer is 16.2 kilohertz or less. The traps flip that to 'or more', or change the unit to hertz or megahertz.

params.title: Highest PRF for 10 nautical miles
steps: Twice the range: half the PRF

onScreen: Twice the range, half the PRF
scenes.narration: Double the range to 10 nautical miles. The round trip is 10 times 12.34, or 123.4 microseconds. A million microseconds divided by 123.4 is about 8.1 thousand, so the PRF should be approximately 8.1 kilohertz or less. Notice what happened: twice the range means twice the wait, so only half as many pulses fit into each second. The traps here include 900 hertz, 18.1 kilohertz or more, and 120.3 microseconds, which isn't even a frequency.

Here are the first 2 again: 5 miles allows up to 16.2 kilohertz, and 10 miles about 8.1. The same 2 steps work for any range. For 30 nautical miles, the round trip is 30 times 12.34, or 370.2 microseconds. A million divided by 370.2 is about 2.7 thousand, so the PRF should be 2.7 kilohertz or less. For 100 nautical miles, the round trip is 100 times 12.34, or 1,234 microseconds, which is 1.234 thousandths of a second. 1 divided by that is about 810, so the PRF should be 810 hertz or less. The takeaway for the whole table: the longer the range, the lower the highest PRF, and the answer is always 'or less'.

params.title: What sets the size of an echo
items: Transmitted power: send more, and more comes back
Antenna effective area: a bigger antenna catches more of the echo
Transmit and receive losses: energy lost along the way

scenes.narration: Timing decides how far out the radar can look. But a distant echo is useless if it's too weak to see. So what controls the size of the target echo? The radar range equation, the formula engineers use for echo strength, lists 5 things, and the first 3 belong to the radar itself. Transmitted power: send more, and more comes back. Antenna effective area: a bigger antenna catches more of the returning echo. And transmit and receive losses: energy lost along the way, in the cables and in the waveguides, the metal pipes that carry microwaves.

params.title: Echo size: the target and its range
items: The target's RADAR cross section: how well it reflects
Range to target: the echo fades very fast with distance
Exam answer: power, effective area, losses, cross section, range
Not receiver gain: it amplifies the echo only after it arrives

scenes.narration: The other 2 depend on the target and where it is. The target's RADAR cross section is how well it reflects, which depends on its size, shape and material. And range to target: the pulse spreads out on the way there, and the echo spreads out again on the way back, so echoes fade very quickly with distance. So the exam's answer lists transmitted power, antenna effective area, transmit and receive losses, RADAR cross section and range to target. Watch for receiver gain in the wrong choices. Gain is how much the receiver amplifies, and it only strengthens an echo after it arrives, so it doesn't set the echo's size.

params.title: What limits maximum range?
rows: Affects it: weakened by air and rain
Affects it: echoes must return in time
Affects it: the weakest echo it can detect
No effect: it limits the minimum range

onScreen: Recovery time: no effect; limits minimum range
scenes.narration: Echo strength is only part of what sets maximum range, how far a radar can see. The carrier frequency matters, because higher frequencies are weakened more by air and rain. So does the PRF: fire too often, and distant echoes come back too late. And so does receiver sensitivity: the fainter the echo it can detect, the farther it can see. Recovery time is different. The duplexer's switch, the TR tube, short for transmit-receive tube, shields the receiver during each pulse. Recovery time is how quickly the TR tube and receiver regain full sensitivity afterward. Only echoes from very close targets arrive during that recovery. So recovery time has no effect on maximum range: it limits the minimum range instead.

params.title: Minimum range and pulse width
labels: A very close target: its echo returns while the pulse is still going out
Blind zone: about 150 m for every µs of pulse width
A 0.5 µs pulse: about 75 m minimum range
Minimum range is set by the transmitted pulse width

onScreen: Close echo returns during the pulse
Blind zone: about 150 m per µs of pulse width
Minimum range set by pulse width
scenes.narration: What mainly sets the minimum range, how close a radar can see? A very close target's echo returns almost instantly, while the pulse is still going out. During the pulse the receiver is shut off, so that echo is never heard. The inner circle shows that blind zone, and its size depends on how long the pulse lasts. At 150 meters per microsecond, every microsecond of pulse width hides about 150 meters of range, and a 0.5 microsecond pulse gives a minimum range of about 75 meters. So the minimum range of a RADAR is determined by the transmitted pulse width. The PRF, the PRR and the transmitter frequency are traps: the PRF and PRR limit the maximum range instead.

params.title: Short range: narrow pulses, fast rate
labels: Narrow pulses: small minimum range
Narrow pulses: fine range resolution
Close echoes return quickly: pulses can be sent often
Short range RADARs: narrow pulses at a fast rate

onScreen: Narrow pulses at a fast rate
scenes.narration: So what pulses suit a radar used at short range, say, entering a harbor? Narrow pulses. A narrow pulse gives a small minimum range, so close-in buoys and boats aren't lost in the blind zone. It also gives fine range resolution: the ability to show 2 targets on the same bearing, close together in range, as 2 separate echoes instead of a single long smear. And because close-in echoes return quickly, the radar doesn't need to wait long between pulses, so it can send them at a fast rate. More pulses also means more hits on each target. So short range RADARs most likely transmit narrow pulses at a fast rate.

params.title: Long range: wide pulses, lower PRR
labels: Wide pulses: more energy on a distant target
Lower PRR: time for distant echoes to return
Lower PRR also keeps duty cycle and average power in limits
Lower PRR with wider pulse width

onScreen: Lower PRR: time for distant echoes
Duty cycle and average power in limits
Lower PRR with wider pulse width
scenes.narration: At long range, the needs flip. A distant echo is weak, so the radar uses wider pulses to put more energy on the target. And distant echoes take longer to return, so it lowers the pulse repetition rate to give them time. There's another reason, too. Remember that duty cycle is pulse width times PRF. Widen the pulses but keep firing just as often, and the duty cycle, and with it the magnetron's average power, would climb past what the tube can safely handle. So the relationship between pulse repetition rate and pulse width is: lower PRR with wider pulse width. Short range settings do the opposite: narrow pulses at a higher PRR.

params.title: Seeing small targets
items: A small target reflects very little energy
Its echo must stand out above receiver noise
Energy in a pulse = power × time
Best: a long pulse width with high output power

scenes.narration: What about a small target, like a small boat or a buoy far out? It reflects very little energy, so the question is whether its echo can stand out above receiver noise, the faint hiss of random electrical signals that every receiver hears. The energy in each pulse is its power multiplied by how long it lasts. So small targets are best detected using a long pulse width with high output power. That puts the most energy on the target and gives the strongest echo. The trap answers, short pulses at a fast rate or J band, just another band of frequencies, don't add energy, so 'all of these' is wrong too.

onScreen: Short range: narrow pulses, fast rate
Long range: wide pulses, slower rate
Width and rate move opposite ways
scenes.narration: Let's put short range and long range side by side. Short range uses narrow pulses, long range uses wide ones. Short range sends them at a fast rate, long range at a slower one. The reasons: short range wants a small minimum range and fine detail, while long range wants more energy on distant targets and time for their echoes to return. Many marine radars switch between settings like these automatically when you change the range scale, how far out the screen shows. The takeaway: pulse width and pulse rate move in opposite directions.

callouts.label: From waveguide: echoes arrive through a metal pipe for microwaves
Crystal detector: the mixer
The block below it: the local oscillator, feeding the mixer
IF amplifier, 30 or 40 MHz: the main amplifier
Detector and video amplifier: recover the pulses for the CRT screen

scenes.narration: With the pulses chosen, let's open up the receiver, using the exam's Figure 8A1. Echoes arrive at top left from the waveguide. After passing block 46, which we'll come back to, they reach the crystal detector, acting here as the mixer. Just below it, the local oscillator feeds in its steady signal. The mixer's output is the difference between the 2 frequencies, called the IF, or intermediate frequency: here 30 or 40 megahertz, far below the echo's gigahertz and much easier to amplify. The IF amplifier builds it up. The detector strips away the radio wave, leaving just the outline of each pulse, and the video amplifier strengthens those pulses for the CRT, the cathode ray tube screen.

callouts.label: Block 46: the TR box, between the waveguide and the crystal
During each pulse, its TR tube fires and shields the crystal
Between pulses, it passes the weak echoes through
Not the ATR box: that one keeps echoes out of the transmitter

onScreen: Fires during the pulse to protect the crystal
scenes.narration: What is block 46? It sits between the waveguide and the crystal detector, right where the receiver needs protecting. So block 46 is the TR box, the transmit-receive switch that's part of the duplexer. Inside it is a gas-filled TR tube. When the powerful transmitted pulse arrives, the gas instantly fires, glowing like a tiny neon sign, and closes the path like a gate, turning the pulse away from the fragile crystal. When the pulse ends, the gas goes out, and the weak echoes pass through. The trap answer is the ATR box, anti-transmit-receive. It's the duplexer's other half, which keeps echoes from leaking into the transmitter, and it doesn't sit in front of the crystal.

callouts.label: AFC, automatic frequency control: retunes the local oscillator
Block 47: the RF attenuator, fed straight from the magnetron
It cuts a sample of the pulse down to a safe level
The sample feeds the AFC mixer, the next block along

onScreen: Block 47: RF attenuator from the magnetron
scenes.narration: Now the figure's bottom row: the AFC, automatic frequency control. A magnetron's frequency drifts as it warms up. The local oscillator must follow it, so the IF stays where the IF amplifier is tuned; otherwise the echoes would drift out of tune and fade. The AFC compares the 2 frequencies and retunes the local oscillator, using a sample of the magnetron's pulse. Block 47, fed straight from the magnetron, is the RF attenuator. RF means radio frequency, and an attenuator reduces signal strength, like sunglasses for radio waves. It cuts a sample of the powerful transmitter output down to a safe level for the AFC mixer. The ATR box, TR box and crystal detector are the wrong choices.

params.title: Diodes and the silicon crystal
items: Diode: lets current flow one way only, like a one-way valve
Semiconductor: a material such as silicon, between a conductor and an insulator
Point-contact diode: a fine wire touching a silicon crystal
The tiny contact handles microwaves, but it is fragile

onScreen: Diode: a one-way valve for current
scenes.narration: Back on the top row, the crystal detector is a type of diode, so let's see what that is. A diode lets current flow through it in one direction only, like a one-way valve in a water pipe. Most diodes are made of a semiconductor such as silicon: a material that conducts electricity better than an insulator like glass, but not as well as a metal. The radar's mixer crystal is a special kind called a point-contact diode. A fine metal wire just touches a tiny chip of silicon crystal. That tiny contact point is what lets it work at microwave frequencies, but it also makes it very fragile.

params.title: Handling silicon crystals
items: Very sensitive to static electric charges
Store them wrapped in lead foil
They tolerate only very low currents
On the exam: all of these

scenes.narration: Because they're so fragile, silicon crystals need careful handling, and the exam asks about every caution at once. They're very sensitive to static electric charges: the tiny spark you get from touching a doorknob can destroy one. They should be wrapped in lead foil for storage, which shields them from stray charges and fields. And they tolerate only very low currents. So when the exam lists all 3 cautions, the answer is all of these.

params.title: How much current a crystal takes

marks.label: 15 mA
marks.note: Trap: would burn out the junction

marks.label: 50 mA
marks.note: Trap: would burn out the junction

marks.label: 100 mA
marks.note: Trap: would burn out the junction

scenes.narration: How low is that current? Small currents are measured in milliamps. A milliamp is one thousandth of an amp. A typical current for a silicon crystal in a RADAR mixer or detector circuit is 3 milliamps. Much higher currents, such as the trap answers of 15, 50 or 100 milliamps, would burn out the tiny junction where the wire meets the crystal.

params.title: What an oscillator needs
labels: Oscillator: makes a steady wave on its own
A resonator sets the frequency
An energy source makes up the losses on each cycle
Microwave resonator: a resonant cavity, a hollow metal box

onScreen: Oscillator: a steady wave on its own
Resonant cavity: a hollow metal box
scenes.narration: That covers the receiver's front end. Now, its local oscillator. How does any oscillator keep a wave going by itself? Think of a child on a swing. The swing has a natural rhythm, set by the length of its ropes. Push in time with that rhythm, and the swinging keeps going. An oscillator needs the same 2 things: a resonator that sets the frequency, and a source of energy that tops up what's lost on each cycle. At microwave frequencies, the resonator is usually a resonant cavity: a hollow metal box that rings at just 1 frequency, the way a bottle hums a single note when you blow across it. A smaller cavity rings at a higher frequency.

blocks.label: Mixer
blocks.note: Its loading pulls the frequency slightly

scenes.narration: A common solid-state local oscillator is the Gunn oscillator: a small device called a Gunn diode, mounted inside a resonant cavity. Which part sets the frequency? The basic frequency-determining element in a Gunn oscillator is the resonant cavity. The diode is the energy source. It supplies negative resistance. Ordinary resistance, a material's opposition to current, soaks up energy as heat and would let the ringing die away. Negative resistance does the opposite: it feeds energy in, keeping the oscillation going. The loading by the mixer it feeds, or a change in supply voltage, only pulls the frequency slightly. So on the exam, pick the cavity, not the power supply voltage, the type of semiconductor, or the loading.

params.title: How a Gunn diode works
items: No PN junction, unlike an ordinary diode
A single chip of gallium arsenide
At high fields, electrons shift to a slower energy band
More voltage, less current: negative resistance
It uses both negative resistance and the bulk effect

onScreen: Electrons shift to a slower band
scenes.narration: How does a Gunn diode make negative resistance? An ordinary diode has a PN junction, a boundary where 2 different kinds of semiconductor meet. A Gunn diode has no junction: it's a single chip of 1 semiconductor, gallium arsenide. Push the voltage across it high enough, and electrons throughout the material jump into a different energy band, where they move more slowly. So raising the voltage actually lowers the current: negative resistance. Because it happens throughout the bulk of the material, not at a junction, it's called the bulk effect. So a Gunn diode oscillator takes advantage of both negative resistance and the bulk effect. Pick the choice with both, not either alone, and not avalanche transit time.

params.title: The reflex klystron
items: A vacuum tube oscillator, often the local oscillator
An electron beam passes through a resonant cavity
A negative repeller turns the electrons back through it in bunches
Cavity dimensions set the primary operating frequency
Coarse tuning: mechanically change the cavity's size

scenes.narration: The older kind of local oscillator is the reflex klystron, a vacuum tube. A beam of electrons shoots through a resonant cavity toward a plate called the repeller, held at a negative voltage. Since like charges push each other away, the repeller turns the electrons around and sends them back through the cavity, now gathered into bunches. If the bunches arrive in step with the cavity's ringing, they give it energy and keep it oscillating. As with the Gunn oscillator, the primary operating frequency of a reflex klystron is controlled by the dimensions of its resonant cavity. Coarse tuning mechanically changes those dimensions, for example by flexing a cavity wall. Grid and repeller voltages are the trap answers.

params.title: Tuning a reflex klystron
rows: Return time of the electron bunches
Fine tuning; what the AFC adjusts

scenes.narration: So the cavity gives coarse tuning. How are fine adjustments made? By varying the repeller voltage. A slightly different repeller voltage changes how long the electron bunches take to turn around and return to the cavity. That nudges the frequency up or down a little, smoothly and with no moving parts. And that's exactly what the AFC circuits in Figure 8A1 adjust: the AFC output changes the klystron's repeller voltage to keep it in step with the magnetron. On the exam, the flexible cavity wall is coarse tuning, and 'adjusting the AFC control system' is wrong: the AFC is what does the adjusting, by changing the repeller voltage.

params.title: Resistance and Ohm's law
items: Resistance: opposition to current, measured in ohms (Ω)
Resistor: a part made to have a chosen resistance
Ohm's law: I = E ÷ R
Current (I) = voltage (E) ÷ resistance (R)

scenes.narration: Remember the synchronizer's trigger pulses and the indicator's sweep? Next come circuits that make them. They're built from resistors and capacitors, so let's meet those first. Resistance, which came up with the Gunn diode, is opposition to current, measured in ohms. In the water picture, it's a narrow section of pipe that holds back the flow. A resistor is a part made to have a chosen resistance. Voltage, current and resistance are tied together by Ohm's law: current equals voltage divided by resistance. In symbols, I equals E divided by R, where I is current, E is voltage, and R is resistance. More push means more current, and more resistance means less.

params.title: Capacitors and the RC time constant
steps: A capacitor stores charge, like a small tank
It drains through a resistor, not instantly
Bigger R or bigger C: slower draining
params.answer: Time constant T = R × C, in seconds

scenes.narration: The other building block is the capacitor, a part that stores electric charge, like a small tank that fills with water. Let a charged capacitor drain through a resistor, and it doesn't empty all at once. It drains quickly at first, then more and more slowly, like a tank emptying through a narrow pipe. A bigger tank or a narrower pipe takes longer. That time is measured by the RC time constant: T equals R times C, the resistance in ohms times the capacitance, the size of the tank, measured in farads. T comes out in seconds. Double either one, and the draining takes twice as long. So choosing a resistor and a capacitor sets a time.

params.title: The blocking oscillator
labels: Conducts for one brief, sharp pulse
Then blocked: cut off while C discharges through R
Off time set by T = R × C
So R and C set the pulse repetition rate

onScreen: R and C set the pulse rate
scenes.narration: Here's a circuit that puts the time constant to work: the blocking oscillator. It's a simple pulse generator that can supply a radar's trigger pulses. It switches on hard for a single brief, sharp pulse. That pulse leaves its timing capacitor charged, and the charge holds the circuit switched off, or blocked, while the capacitor drains away through a resistor. Once it has drained enough, the circuit fires again. So the off time, and with it the pulse repetition rate, is set by the RC time constant. That's why blocking oscillators operate on the formula T equals R times C. The trap, I equals E over R, is Ohm's law, which doesn't set any timing.

params.title: The phantastron: a precise ramp
labels: Triggered by an external pulse
One-shot: one ramp per trigger
A very linear ramp voltage of precisely settable length
Used for range-marker and delay timing

scenes.narration: Trigger pulses are one timing job. The other is the indicator's sweep, which needs a ramp: a voltage rising at a perfectly steady rate, so equal distances on the screen mean equal times and ranges. A classic ramp maker is the phantastron, a triggered, one-shot sweep generator: each trigger from an outside source makes it produce exactly 1 ramp. That ramp is very linear, rising in a straight line, and its length can be set precisely, which suits range-marker and delay timing, placing a mark on the screen at an exact range. So the phantastron can develop a linear ramp voltage when triggered by an external source. It doesn't stabilize the magnetron, prevent receiver saturation or control the repeller voltage.

params.title: Analog and digital
labels: Analog: any value, like the echoes from the receiver
Digital, drawn here: only 2 levels, high and low
High = 1, low = 0: binary digits, or bits
Radars process echoes as numbers

scenes.narration: Modern radars also contain digital circuits, so here's the idea behind them. The echoes coming out of the receiver are analog: a voltage that can rise and fall smoothly to any value. A digital circuit works with just 2 levels, high and low, like a light switch that's either on or off. High stands for 1 and low stands for 0. These 1s and 0s are binary digits, or bits, and groups of bits can stand for any number. Turning echoes into numbers lets a radar's computer circuits clean up clutter, the unwanted echoes from waves and rain, track targets and draw a sharp display.

blocks.label: Output buffer
blocks.note: Keeps the load from draining it

scenes.narration: To turn an analog voltage into a number, a converter must measure it, and the voltage has to hold still while it does. That's the job of a sample-and-hold circuit: it freezes a snapshot of the voltage. A basic sample-and-hold circuit contains an analog switch, a capacitor, amplifiers, and input and output buffers. A buffer is a helper amplifier that passes a voltage along unchanged while supplying plenty of current. The input buffer charges the hold capacitor quickly. While the analog switch is closed, it connects the signal to the capacitor, which follows it. When the switch opens, the capacitor holds its voltage: the snapshot. The output buffer reads it without draining it. Shorter choices leave parts out.

params.title: Analog-to-digital conversion methods
rows: Not a method: dynamic range is a specification

onScreen: Dynamic range: a specification, not a method
scenes.narration: The circuit that does the measuring is an analog-to-digital converter, or ADC. There are several ways to build one, and the exam asks which of these is not a method of analog-to-digital conversion. Delta-sigma conversion, switched-capacitor conversion and dual-slope integration are all genuine methods. You don't need to know how each one works, just that they're real. Dynamic-range conversion is the odd one out. Dynamic range is a specification: the span from the weakest to the strongest signal a converter can handle. It describes a converter, but it isn't a way of converting.

params.title: The transistor as a switch
items: Transistor: a small current or voltage controls a larger current
Bipolar transistor: base, collector and emitter
Saturated: switched fully on
Off, or cut off: no current flows
MOSFET: a transistor switched by a voltage instead of a current

scenes.narration: Once the echoes are numbers, digital circuits do the work, and those are built from transistors. Here's what you need to know about them. A transistor is a semiconductor part that works like an electrically controlled switch. In the common bipolar type, a small current into one lead, the base, controls a much larger current between the other 2 leads, the collector and the emitter. Give the base enough current, and the transistor is switched fully on, which is called saturated. Take it away, and the transistor is off, or cut off, and no current flows. Another kind, the MOSFET, short for metal-oxide semiconductor field-effect transistor, is switched by a voltage instead of a current.

Transistors are combined into logic gates, small circuits that make simple decisions about highs and lows. The one the exam uses is the NAND gate, short for not-and. Here's its truth table, a list of every input combination and the output it gives. With both inputs low, the output is high. With either input low, the output is still high. Only when both inputs are high does the output go low. Keep that rule in mind: a NAND gate's output is low only when every input is high.

params.title: TTL and CMOS NAND gates compared
rows: Pairs of P- and N-channel MOSFETs
Upper transistor of its totem-pole output

scenes.narration: Logic gates come in families. TTL, transistor-transistor logic, is built from bipolar transistors. CMOS, complementary metal-oxide semiconductor, is built from matched pairs of MOSFETs of 2 opposite types, P-channel and N-channel, which is what complementary means. Every gate output must be driven high or low. When a transistor actively switches on to pull the output high, that's called active pull-up. TTL does it with the upper transistor of its totem-pole output: 2 transistors stacked like a totem pole, one pulling up and one pulling down. CMOS does it with its P-channel MOSFETs. So both have active pull-up. Neither is a three-state device, whose output can also disconnect. And their input currents differ greatly, so they don't have comparable input sourcing.

params.title: Why CMOS power rises with frequency
labels: Holding still: CMOS draws almost no current
Each switch charges or discharges the load capacitance
More switching per second: more power
At high frequencies, CMOS uses almost as much power as TTL

onScreen: High frequency: almost as much as TTL
scenes.narration: Those matched pairs give CMOS its big advantage: low power. When a CMOS gate holds still, one transistor of each pair is always off, so almost no current flows. But every wire and input it drives has a little capacitance, the ability to store charge, just like a tiny capacitor. Each time the output switches, that capacitance must be charged or emptied, and that takes current. So the faster it switches, the more power it uses. That's why, at higher operating frequencies, CMOS circuits consume almost as much power as TTL circuits. On the exam, pick that statement over the choices about supply tolerances, unused inputs and sourcing current.

params.title: Figure 8A6: inside a TTL NAND gate

callouts.label: Q<sub>1</sub>: a multi-emitter transistor, one emitter for each input, A and B
Q<sub>1</sub>'s base: fed from the 5 V supply through a resistor
Q<sub>1</sub>'s collector drives the base of Q<sub>2</sub>
Q<sub>3</sub> above, Q<sub>4</sub> below: the totem-pole output

onScreen: Q1's base fed from the supply
scenes.narration: Now let's look inside the other family, TTL. Figure 8A6 shows the circuit of a TTL NAND gate, built from 4 transistors. On the left, Q sub 1 is a multi-emitter transistor: it has 2 emitters, one for each input, A and B. Its base is fed from the 5 volt supply through a resistor, so current is always ready to flow into it. Its collector drives the base of Q sub 2, in the middle. On the right, Q sub 3 above and Q sub 4 below form the totem-pole output you met earlier: one pulls the output high, the other pulls it low.

callouts.label: Either input low: Q<sub>1</sub>'s base current flows out that emitter
Q<sub>1</sub> saturated: its collector pulls Q<sub>2</sub>'s base low
Q<sub>2</sub> off, so the totem pole drives the output high
Either A or B low: Q<sub>1</sub> saturated, Q<sub>2</sub> off

onScreen: Either input low: base current flows out
Q1 saturated, Q2 base pulled low
Either A or B low: Q1 saturated, Q2 off
scenes.narration: Now suppose either input is pulled low, close to 0 volts. The base current of Q sub 1 takes the easy path downhill, flowing out through that low emitter. Q sub 1 is now saturated, fully on, and its collector pulls the base of Q sub 2 low. With no base current, Q sub 2 is off. And with Q sub 2 off, the totem pole drives the output high. That matches the NAND rule: any low input gives a high output. So the exam's answer is: with either A or B low, Q sub 1 is saturated and Q sub 2 is off. The trap reverses it, with Q sub 1 off and Q sub 2 on.

callouts.label: A line driver sends fast digital pulses down a 50 Ω cable
A line receiver picks them up at the far end
Box X: a 51-ohm resistor terminating the cable
51 Ω: the nearest standard value to the cable's 50 Ω
No reflections to distort the pulses

onScreen: Line receiver at the far end
scenes.narration: Between circuit boards, a gate's pulses often travel over coaxial cable: a center wire inside a tube-shaped shield. In Figure 8A3, a line driver sends pulses down a 50 ohm cable to a line receiver. 50 ohms is the cable's characteristic impedance, where impedance means opposition to changing signals, measured in ohms. A cable behaves well only if its far end is connected to a resistance equal to that impedance. Otherwise part of each pulse bounces back, like a wave on a rope tied to a wall, distorting the pulses. Box X is the fix: a 51-ohm resistor terminating the cable at the receiving end. 51 ohms, the nearest standard value to 50, absorbs each pulse instead of reflecting it.

params.title: The D-type flip-flop
items: Flip-flop: a circuit that remembers 1 bit
D-type: on each rising clock edge, Q copies the D input
Q̄ (Q bar): always the opposite of Q
Preset and clear: force Q high or low; often active low
Reset: Q low, Q̄ high

onScreen: Reset: Q low, Q bar high
scenes.narration: Gates make decisions, but they don't remember anything. For memory, digital circuits use the flip-flop, a circuit that remembers 1 bit. The D-type flip-flop has a data input, D, and a clock input, which receives timing pulses. Each time the clock rises from low to high, the flip-flop copies whatever is on D to its output, Q, and holds it until the next rising edge. A second output, Q bar, is always the opposite of Q. Many flip-flops also have preset and clear inputs, which force Q high or low whatever the clock does. These are often active low, meaning they act only when pulled low. And in the reset state, Q is low and Q bar is high.

callouts.label: Pins 1 and 4, clear and preset, held high: out of the way
Both flip-flops start reset: Q low, Q̄ high
Left flip-flop: Q̄ on pin 6 feeds its own D input, pin 2
Pin 2 is high, so Clk A loads a high: pin 5 goes high

onScreen: Both reset: Q low, Q bar high
scenes.narration: Figure 8A4 puts 2 D-type flip-flops to work. The exam tells you pins 1 and 4 are high and both flip-flops start in the reset state. Pins 1 and 4 are the left flip-flop's clear and preset inputs. They're active low, so holding them high keeps them out of the way. And since both start reset, each Q is low and each Q bar is high. Now look at the left flip-flop. Its Q bar output, pin 6, is wired back to its own D input, pin 2. Q bar is high, so pin 2 is high. When the first clock cycle arrives on clock A, the flip-flop copies that high to Q. So pin 5 goes high.

callouts.label: Pin 5, now high, drives the right flip-flop's D input, pin 12
Clk B loads that high into the right flip-flop
Its Q output, pin 9, goes high
Result: pin 5 high and pin 9 high

scenes.narration: Now follow pin 5 to the right. It drives the right flip-flop's D input on pin 12, so pin 12 is now high. Next comes 1 cycle on clock B. The right flip-flop copies its high D input to its Q output, so pin 9 goes high. Pin 5 stays high, because the left flip-flop hasn't been clocked again. So after 1 cycle of clock A followed by 1 cycle of clock B, the answer is pin 5 high and pin 9 high. The trick is to take it one clock at a time, and always read D just before the clock edge.

callouts.label: Inputs: OE̅ (output enable, active low), CP (clock), Dn (data)
Clock rising: D high gives Q low; D low gives Q high
Q takes the opposite of D: an inverting D-type flip-flop
OE̅ high: output Z, high impedance, so it is 3-state
D-type flip-flop, 3-state, inverting

onScreen: OE bar, CP and Dn inputs
scenes.narration: Figure 8A8 is the truth table of another flip-flop, a part on a RADAR circuit board. The inputs are OE bar, the output enable, which is active low; CP, the clock; and D n, the data input. The output is Q n. In the first 2 rows, output enable is low and the clock goes from low to high. A high D gives a low Q, and a low D gives a high Q, so it's a D-type flip-flop that inverts. With no clock edge, nothing changes. In the bottom row, output enable is high, and the output goes to Z, the high-impedance state: disconnected. High, low or disconnected makes 3 states. So it's a D-type flip-flop, 3-state, inverting.

params.title: Figure 8A2: buses and the outside world

callouts.label: Internal bus: shared wires linking the blocks
Shared, so it carries one transfer at a time
Memory and I/O interface: the only block on the memory and I/O bus
So the memory and I/O communicate with peripherals

onScreen: Memory and I/O interface on the outside bus
Memory and I/O communicate with peripherals
scenes.narration: Thousands of gates and flip-flops together make a microprocessor, the small computer chip that runs a radar's digital functions. Figure 8A2 shows one. The long double-headed arrow near the top is the internal bus, a set of shared wires that carries data between the blocks inside the chip. Because it's shared, it carries one transfer at a time: the units take turns, they don't all use it at once. At the right is the memory and I-O interface, I-O meaning input-output. It's the only block connected to the outside memory and I-O bus. So it's the memory and I-O that communicate with peripherals, the devices outside the processor, such as memory chips, displays and keyboards.

callouts.label: Registers: small, fast storage spots inside the chip
General registers D0 to D7 and A0 to A7, plus the TEMP register
ALU: executes arithmetic manipulations on their data
The result goes back over the internal bus
Control unit: decodes instructions; it does no arithmetic

scenes.narration: Inside, data waits in registers: small, fast storage spots. The general registers, labeled D 0 to D 7 and A 0 to A 7, hold the numbers being worked on, and the TEMP register holds a temporary value. Below them sits the ALU, the arithmetic logic unit. The ALU executes arithmetic manipulations: it takes data from the general registers and the TEMP register, adds, subtracts or compares it, and returns the result over the internal bus. The ALU doesn't decode instructions. That's the job of the control unit, on the right, which reads each program instruction and directs the other blocks, but does no arithmetic itself.

callouts.label: Address: the number of a location in memory
Address pointer: a register holding an address
D registers hold data; A registers hold addresses
So address pointers are in the general registers

scenes.narration: One more question on this figure. Every location in memory has a number, called its address, like a house number on a street. A register that holds an address, so the processor knows where to find its data, is called an address pointer. Look at the general registers again: D 0 to D 7 are data registers, and A 0 to A 7 are address registers. So address pointers are contained in the general registers. The traps put address pointers in the control unit, or say the ALU does address decoding, or that the general registers or control unit do the arithmetic. Remember: the ALU calculates, the control unit decodes instructions, and the general registers hold data and addresses.

callouts.label: The 12 V battery reverse-biases the photodiode: the normal way to run it
Reverse-biased: the diode blocks, except a tiny dark current
Light creates electron-hole pairs in the junction
More light, more diode current

scenes.narration: Let's finish with 2 circuits that work with light. In Figure 8A5, a photodiode, a diode that responds to light, is connected to a meter and a 12 volt battery. Remember that a diode is a one-way valve. Here the battery is connected the blocking way round, which is called reverse bias. That's the normal way to run a photodiode, not a wiring mistake. In the dark, only a tiny leakage current flows, called dark current. When light strikes the junction, it knocks electrons loose, each leaving behind a gap called a hole, and these electron-hole pairs carry current. So more light means more diode current, and the meter reads higher.

params.title: Figure 8A7: why an LED needs a resistor

callouts.label: LED: a light-emitting diode, lit by forward current
Once lit, its voltage stays almost fixed: here 1.9 V
Alone on the 5 V supply, its current would climb until it burned out
R<sub>S</sub>: a series resistor, in the same path, limits the current

onScreen: Lit LED: about 1.9 V, almost fixed
R S: series resistor limits the current
scenes.narration: The second circuit works the other way round: instead of sensing light, it makes it. In Figure 8A7, an LED, a light-emitting diode, glows when current flows through it the forward way. Once an LED is lit, the voltage across it stays almost fixed, here 1.9 volts. So it can't limit its own current. Connect it straight to the 5 volt supply, and its current would climb until it burned out. That's why it has a series resistor, R sub S. Series means in the same path, so all of the LED's current must pass through the resistor, and the resistor sets how much flows.

params.title: Figure 8A7: the LED series resistor
steps: Voltage across R<sub>S</sub>: 5 V − 1.9 V = 3.1 V

scenes.narration: So what value should R sub S be? The resistor must drop whatever voltage the LED doesn't. The supply is 5 volts and the LED drops 1.9, so the resistor drops 5 minus 1.9, which is 3.1 volts. The current must not exceed the LED's maximum forward current, 40 milliamps, or 0.040 amperes, since a milliamp is a thousandth of an amp. Now Ohm's law, turned around: resistance equals voltage divided by current. 3.1 volts divided by 0.040 amperes is 77.5 ohms, so the answer is about 77 ohms. Watch for the 155 ohm trap: twice the resistance, it would let only half the current flow.

params.title: Key facts to remember
items: 1 RADAR mile = 12.34 µs; range: 150 meters per microsecond
Duty cycle = PW × PRF; P<sub>avg</sub> = P<sub>pk</sub> × PW × PRF
Highest PRF = 1 ÷ round trip time; minimum range set by pulse width
S-band 2 to 4 GHz, better in weather; X-band 8 to 12 GHz, better bearing
Synchronizer: timing. Duplexer: 1 antenna. TR box: protects the crystal

onScreen: RADAR mile 12.34 µs; 150 m per µs
scenes.narration: To wrap up, 5 things to remember. Timing: a RADAR mile is 12.34 microseconds out and back, and range is measured at 150 meters per microsecond, so echo time divided by 12.34 gives nautical miles, with no halving. Power: duty cycle is pulse width times PRF, and average power is peak power times duty cycle. Range limits: the PRF can be no higher than 1 divided by the round trip time, and the pulse width sets the minimum range. Frequency: S-band, 2 to 4 gigahertz, handles weather better; X-band, 8 to 12 gigahertz, has better bearing resolution. And the parts: the synchronizer controls timing, the duplexer lets 1 antenna transmit and receive, and the TR box protects the receiver's crystal.
